questions.title: Node NotReady: kubelet stopped
questions.question:
ssh cka01001
The worker node node01 is reported as NotReady. Investigate the cause and bring node01 back to the Ready state. Your fix must survive a reboot of node01.
keys: fix must survive reboot (enable the service)
questions.setup:
ssh node01 'systemctl stop kubelet; systemctl disable kubelet' 2>/dev/null
sleep 60
questions.meaning: The kubelet on node01 is switched off; turn it on and make it start automatically.
questions.words:
• kubelet = the node agent that starts pods and reports to the control plane
  • NotReady = the control plane stopped hearing from that kubelet
  • systemctl enable = start the service at every boot

flow.h: NotReady usually means the kubelet on that node is not talking. If it still says Ready, wait 30 s and run it again. The control plane waits ~50 s before marking a node NotReady.

steps.title: Log in to node01 and become root

flow.h: The kubelet runs on the node itself, not as a pod. systemctl changes need root. The real exam requires sudo -i. Killercoda is already root, so it changes nothing there.
Shows the kubelet is stopped and will not start at boot.

steps.title: Start it and enable it at boot

flow.h: enable = survives reboot, --now = start right away.
Two exits: one leaves root, one leaves node01. Wait up to 30s for the node to report Ready.

questions.mug:
kubectl get nodes
ssh node01
sudo -i
systemctl status kubelet --no-pager
systemctl enable --now kubelet
systemctl is-enabled kubelet
exit
exit
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get nodes
ssh node01 systemctl is-enabled kubelet

pic.say: The kubelet on node01 is switched off; turn it on and make it start automatically. Words you need: kubelet = the node agent that starts pods and reports to the control plane; NotReady = the control plane stopped hearing from that kubelet; systemctl enable = start the service at every boot.

story.broken: The cook (kubelet) at table node01 stopped and won't come back after a reboot.
story.fix: ssh node01; systemctl enable --now kubelet — the cook is back, also after reboots.

world.goal:
📝 Bring node01 (Team Alpha) back to Ready.
Fix must survive a reboot.

scenes.say: Welcome to your software company. Upstairs is the leadership room: the control plane. Jira, the API server, takes every request and checks permissions. Jira's database, etcd, holds the truth. The work assigner, the scheduler, gives each new work item to a team with capacity. And the Release Train Engineer, the controller manager, keeps reality matching the plan.

Downstairs is Team Alpha's room: node zero one. The team lead, the container runtime, gets the developers working. And the Scrum Master, the kubelet, takes the assigned work, and at every sync reports to Jira: team healthy!
scenes.sub: kubelet = Scrum Master → reports "team healthy" at every sync

scenes.say: But today, the Scrum Master doesn't show up. No sync, no report. After forty seconds, the Release Train Engineer marks Team Alpha as not reporting: node zero one, Not Ready. And the work assigner stops giving the team new work.
scenes.sub: No report for 40 s → node01 NotReady → no new work

scenes.say: Your exam task: bring node zero one back to Ready. And the fix must survive a reboot. Remember that last part.
Quick question. Why is node zero one Not Ready?

quiz.t: 🧑‍🔧 The Team Lead (container runtime) is off sick
quiz.fb: Not quite. Without the team lead the work would stall, but the Scrum Master would still report. Nobody is reporting at all.

quiz.t: 🧑‍💼 The Scrum Master (kubelet) isn't doing the job
quiz.fb: Exactly! No Scrum Master, no team healthy report, so the team is marked Not Ready.
Not quite. If Jira were down, nobody could see anything, not even k get nodes.

scenes.say: So go to the team's room. S S H node zero one. Your terminal now works inside Team Alpha's room. Look at the prompt: it says node zero one.
scenes.sub: ssh node01 = walk into Team Alpha's room

scenes.say: Every role in the room has an official assignment. That's system control. System control status kubelet asks: is the Scrum Master doing the job? Answer: inactive, dead. Nobody is.
scenes.sub: systemctl = role assignment · status = is anyone doing the job?

scenes.roster: kubelet · active (running) · covering this sprint only
scenes.say: Easy fix: system control start kubelet. Someone covers the role for this sprint. The Scrum Master reports again, Team Alpha is Ready. Done? Not so fast.
scenes.sub: systemctl start = cover the role… this sprint only

scenes.say: Twist! Next week there's a reorg. That's a reboot. And Team Alpha has no Scrum Master again! Why? Start only covered the role for one sprint. Nobody was officially assigned.
scenes.sub: TWIST: reorg (reboot) → no Scrum Master again

scenes.say: So which command officially assigns the Scrum Master, and starts the job right now?

quiz.fb: That's the trap we just fell into. Start only covers this sprint.
Yes! Enable makes the assignment official, so it survives every reorg. Dash dash now also starts it right away.
That command doesn't exist. And kubectl only talks to Jira, not to the role assignments in the team room.

scenes.say: System control enable, dash dash now, kubelet. Enable: officially assigned, so the role survives every reorg. Dash dash now: start right now.
scenes.sub: enable = official, survives reboots · --now = right now

scenes.say: Another reorg. And this time? The Scrum Master is still there. The fix survives a reboot.
scenes.sub: Reorg again → Scrum Master still there ✓

scenes.say: Go back to the leadership room with exit, and check Jira with k get nodes. Node zero one: Ready. Task done!
scenes.sub: exit = back to leadership · k get nodes = check Jira

scenes.say: Remember: Not Ready means the Scrum Master, the kubelet, isn't doing the job. Go to the team with S S H. Check with status. And never just start it: enable dash dash now, so it survives the reorg.
scenes.sub: NotReady → ssh → status → enable --now → exit → get nodes

steps.do: Go to Team Alpha's room and check the Scrum Master
Assign officially and start now, then go back

coach.pattern: Node NotReady → ssh → kubelet stopped → enable --now

clues.means: Run this first — every task is on its own host

clues.q: Your fix must survive a reboot of node01
clues.means: systemctl enable (with --now to also start it)

traps.do: Run `systemctl enable --now kubelet`. A plain start is lost after reboot. Check with `systemctl is-enabled kubelet`.
`ssh cka01001` first, because each exam task runs on its own cluster
Run `sudo -i` right after `ssh node01`. The exam user is not root. Without root, systemctl says Access denied.

traps.dont: Running `k get nodes` while still on node01
traps.do: Run `exit; exit` to leave root, then node01. Then run `k get nodes`. kubectl works only on the cka01001 host.

memorise: ssh cka01001; k get nodes   # NotReady (wait ~60 s if still Ready)
systemctl enable --now kubelet; systemctl is-enabled kubelet

questions.title: Service has no endpoints
questions.question:
ssh cka01002
In namespace shop the Service cart does not forward traffic to the Pods of Deployment cart. Fix the Service so that it routes to the Deployment's Pods. Do not modify the Deployment.
questions.setup:
kubectl create namespace shop --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: cart, namespace: shop}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: cart}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: cart}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - {name: nginx, image: nginx:1.27-alpine, ports: [{containerPort: 80}]}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: cart, namespace: shop}
spec:
  selector: {app: carts}
  ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 80}]
EOF
questions.meaning: The Service is looking for the wrong Pod label; correct its selector.
questions.words:
• label = a name tag on a Pod (app=cart)
  • selector = the label a Service looks for
  • EndpointSlice = the list of Pod IPs the Service found

flow.t:
NAME          ADDRESSTYPE   PORTS   ENDPOINTS   AGE
cart-xxxxx    IPv4          80      <unset>     1m

flow.h: ENDPOINTS <unset> = no Pod IPs: the Service selector matches no Pod.

flow.t: kubectl -n shop get svc cart -o wide

flow.h: One letter typo in the selector.
Point the Service at the real Pod label.

flow.t: kubectl -n shop run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- -T3 cart

flow.h: A real request proves traffic flows.

questions.mug:
kubectl -n shop get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=cart
kubectl -n shop get pods --show-labels
kubectl -n shop get svc cart -o wide
kubectl -n shop patch svc cart -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"cart"}}}'
kubectl -n shop run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- -T3 cart
kubectl -n shop get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=cart

pic.say: The Service is looking for the wrong Pod label; correct its selector. Words you need: label = a name tag on a Pod (app=cart); selector = the label a Service looks for; EndpointSlice = the list of Pod IPs the Service found.

story.broken: Phone number cart (Service) looks for the wrong label, so it rings no cart dishes.
story.fix: Edit the Service selector to match the cart pods' labels; leave the Deployment alone.

coach.pattern: Service has no endpoints → fix selector to match pod labels

clues.q: does not forward traffic to the Pods

clues.means: Don't relabel pods — change the Service only

traps.dont: `k -n shop label pods ...` or editing deployment cart
traps.do: Fix the Service selector with `k -n shop patch svc cart ...`. The task forbids changing the Deployment.

traps.dont: `k -n shop patch svc cart ...` when the selector key is wrong
traps.do: Run `k -n shop edit svc cart` and fix the key. A merge patch adds a second key. That second key must also match.
Add `-n shop` to every command, because the Service and pods live in namespace shop

verify.cmd: k -n shop run tmp --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- -T3 cart

memorise: k -n shop get svc cart -o wide   # SELECTOR

questions.title: Pods stuck Pending (requests too big)
questions.question:
ssh cka01003
The Pods of Deployment reporter in namespace batch stay Pending. Find the reason and fix it so that all replicas are Running. Set the memory request of the container to 128Mi. Keep the number of replicas unchanged.
questions.setup:
kubectl create namespace batch --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: reporter, namespace: batch}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: reporter}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: reporter}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: reporter
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
        resources: {requests: {memory: 64Gi}}
EOF
questions.meaning: The pods ask for more memory than any node has; ask for less.
questions.words:
• request = memory a pod reserves up front
  • scheduler = the part that picks a node with enough free memory
  • Pending = no node chosen yet

flow.h: Pending = scheduler cannot find a node.

flow.t: kubectl -n batch describe pod -l app=reporter | grep -A3 Events
0/2 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient memory, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint ...

flow.h: Events tell why a pod is not scheduled. Ignore the taint part (that is the control plane); Insufficient memory is the cause.

flow.t: kubectl -n batch set resources deploy reporter --requests=memory=128Mi

flow.h: Asks for less memory so a node fits.
New pods replace the old Pending ones.

questions.mug:
kubectl -n batch get pods
kubectl -n batch describe pod -l app=reporter | grep -A3 Events
kubectl -n batch set resources deploy reporter --requests=memory=128Mi
kubectl -n batch get pods
kubectl -n batch get deploy reporter -o jsonpath="{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}"
kubectl -n batch get pods

pic.say: The pods ask for more memory than any node has; ask for less. Words you need: request = memory a pod reserves up front; scheduler = the part that picks a node with enough free memory; Pending = no node chosen yet.

story.broken: Reporter dishes ask for more memory than any table has, so the host can't seat them.
story.fix: kubectl set resources deploy reporter --requests=memory=128Mi — all copies get seats.

coach.pattern: Pod Pending → Insufficient memory → set smaller request

clues.q: Set the memory request of the container to 128Mi
Keep the number of replicas unchanged
clues.means: Don't scale down to make it fit

traps.do: `k -n batch set resources deploy reporter --requests=memory=128Mi`, because the task says keep replicas unchanged
Use `--requests=memory=128Mi`, because the scheduler uses requests to find room for the pods

traps.dont: Leaving an existing memory limit below 128Mi
traps.do: If a limit exists, raise it to at least 128Mi too. A limit below the request is invalid.

memorise: k -n batch describe pod -l app=reporter | grep -A3 Events
k -n batch set resources deploy reporter --requests=memory=128Mi

questions.title: CrashLoop / restarts: wrong liveness probe
questions.question:
ssh cka01004
Deployment api in namespace web keeps restarting its Pods. Identify the cause and fix it. The nginx container listens on port 80. Do not delete the Deployment.
questions.setup:
kubectl create namespace web --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: api, namespace: web}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27-alpine
        ports: [{containerPort: 80}]
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /, port: 8080}
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
          periodSeconds: 3
          failureThreshold: 2
EOF
questions.meaning: The health check knocks on the wrong door (8080) so Kubernetes keeps restarting the pod.
questions.words:
• livenessProbe = a URL the kubelet calls again and again
  • if it fails N times in a row the container is restarted
  • RESTARTS = how many times that happened

flow.h: Growing RESTARTS = something kills the container.

flow.t: kubectl -n web describe pod -l app=api | grep -i -A2 liveness

flow.h: Probe checks port 8080 but nginx uses 80.

flow.t:
In vim find these lines and change 8080 to 80:
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
then press Esc, type :wq, Enter -> deployment.apps/api edited

flow.h: Probe now checks the port nginx really uses. Edit the Deployment, not the Pod.

flow.t: kubectl -n web rollout status deploy api

questions.title: Install cri-dockerd + kernel sysctl
questions.question:
ssh cka01007
Prepare this node for a Docker-based container runtime:
- Install the Debian package /root/cri-dockerd.deb using dpkg.
- Enable and start the cri-docker service.
- Configure these kernel parameters so they persist across reboots (file /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf):
  net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1
  net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
  net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1
  net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 131072
questions.setup:
test -f /root/cri-dockerd.deb || curl -fsSLo /root/cri-dockerd.deb https://github.com/Mirantis/cri-dockerd/releases/download/v0.3.16/cri-dockerd_0.3.16.3-0.ubuntu-jammy_amd64.deb || echo "download failed - check release page"
ls -l /root/cri-dockerd.deb || echo "MISSING: download a cri-dockerd .deb for your Ubuntu from https://github.com/Mirantis/cri-dockerd/releases to /root/cri-dockerd.deb"
questions.meaning: Install a runtime package and turn on 4 Linux network settings permanently. On Killercoda Docker is absent, so cri-docker will not start. The jammy .deb may not match a newer Ubuntu. dpkg, enable and sysctl still practise.
questions.words:
• .deb = an Ubuntu install package (dpkg -i installs it)
  • sysctl = a Linux kernel setting
  • kernel module = a driver loaded with modprobe, needed before some sysctl settings exist

flow.h: dpkg, systemctl and /etc need root. The real exam requires sudo -i. Killercoda is already root. If the file is missing on Killercoda, the setup download failed. Download a .deb from the cri-dockerd releases page. Or just practise the commands.
dpkg installs a local .deb file. If dpkg stops with missing dependencies, run apt-get -f install -y. Then check again. Status iU means unpacked but not configured yet. ii means installed.

flow.t:
Killercoda (no Docker): "Job for cri-docker.service failed" - then: enabled
Exam (Docker present): no error - then: enabled

flow.h: enable = at boot, --now = start now. Without Docker the START fails but the ENABLE still worked; is-enabled proves it.

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' > /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 131072
EOF

flow.h: Files in /etc/sysctl.d survive reboots. Paste the whole block at once, including the final EOF line. Everything between the two EOFs goes into the file.

steps.title: Load the kernel modules now and at every boot

flow.h: bridge-nf-call-iptables only exists when br_netfilter is loaded, nf_conntrack_max needs nf_conntrack. modprobe loads them now. The modules-load.d file loads them after a reboot. So the sysctl settings really persist.
Applies all /etc/sysctl.d files without rebooting.

questions.mug:
sudo -i
ls -l /root/cri-dockerd.deb
dpkg -i /root/cri-dockerd.deb
systemctl enable --now cri-docker.service
systemctl is-enabled cri-docker
cat <<'EOF' > /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 131072
EOF
modprobe br_netfilter
modprobe nf_conntrack
printf 'br_netfilter\nnf_conntrack\n' > /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf
sysctl --system | grep -E "bridge-nf-call-iptables|ip_forward|all.forwarding|conntrack_max"
dpkg -l | grep cri-dockerd
systemctl is-enabled cri-docker
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max
questions.docs: kubernetes.io: Container Runtimes (search: cri-dockerd, sysctl ip_forward)

pic.say: Install a runtime package and turn on 4 Linux network settings permanently. On Killercoda Docker is absent, so cri-docker will not start. The jammy .deb may not match a newer Ubuntu. dpkg, enable and sysctl still practise. Words you need: .deb = an Ubuntu install package (dpkg -i installs it); sysctl = a Linux kernel setting; kernel module = a driver loaded with modprobe, needed before some sysctl settings exist.

story.broken: A table (node) needs the Docker stove adapter cri-dockerd and kernel settings that survive reboots.
story.fix: dpkg -i the .deb, systemctl enable --now cri-docker, write the sysctl file, sysctl --system.

Enable and start the cri-docker service

traps.do: Write the 4 lines to /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf. Then run `sysctl --system`. `sysctl -w` is lost on reboot.
Also write br_netfilter and nf_conntrack into /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf, so they load again after reboot

traps.dont: Save the settings in /etc/sysctl.conf or another file
traps.do: Use exactly /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf, because the grader checks the file the question names

traps.dont: Panic when cri-docker fails to start on Killercoda
traps.do: Check `systemctl is-enabled cri-docker`, because without Docker it cannot start there, but enabling still worked

verify.cmd: dpkg -l | grep cri-dockerd; systemctl is-enabled cri-docker

memorise: systemctl enable --now cri-docker; systemctl is-enabled cri-docker

questions.title: Expose container port + NodePort Service
questions.question:
ssh cka01010
Reconfigure the existing Deployment front-end in namespace front: add a port specification named http exposing port 80/tcp of the existing container nginx.
Create a new Service named front-end-svc of type NodePort exposing the container port http, with nodePort 30080. The Service must reach the Pods of the Deployment.
questions.setup:
kubectl create namespace front --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: front-end, namespace: front}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: front-end}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: front-end}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - {name: nginx, image: nginx:1.27-alpine}
EOF
questions.meaning: Name the container port. Open it to the outside on port 30080 of every node.
questions.words:
• containerPort = the port inside the pod (here named http)
  • port = the Service's own port
  • targetPort = where the Service sends traffic (the name http works)
  • nodePort = the port opened on every node (30000-32767)

flow.h: Names port 80 "http" on the container.
NodePort opens the same port on every node.

steps.title: Test from outside the pod network

flow.t: curl -s http://$(kubectl get node node01 -o jsonpath="{.status.addresses[0].address}"):30080 | head -4

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: front-end-svc, namespace: front}
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector: {app: front-end}
  ports:
  - {name: http, port: 80, targetPort: http, protocol: TCP, nodePort: 30080}
EOF
curl -s http://$(kubectl get node node01 -o jsonpath="{.status.addresses[0].address}"):30080 | head -4
kubectl -n front get svc front-end-svc
kubectl -n front get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=front-end-svc

questions.title: Gateway API: migrate Ingress to Gateway + HTTPRoute
questions.question:
ssh cka01011
Migrate the existing Ingress web in namespace web-app to the Gateway API, keeping HTTPS:
- Create a Gateway named web-gateway using GatewayClass nginx, with an HTTPS listener on port 443 for hostname gateway.web.example. Use the TLS Secret web-tls already referenced by the Ingress.
- Create an HTTPRoute named web-route bound to web-gateway that sends all paths (/) for gateway.web.example to Service web on port 80.
- Delete the Ingress web when done.
keys: listener HTTPS 443, host gateway.web.example, secret web-tls
delete ingress web at the end
questions.setup:
kubectl get crd gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io >/dev/null 2>&1 || kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.2.1/standard-install.yaml
kubectl create namespace web-app --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
openssl req -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -days 365 -subj "/CN=gateway.web.example" -keyout /tmp/web-tls.key -out /tmp/web-tls.crt 2>/dev/null
kubectl -n web-app create secret tls web-tls --cert=/tmp/web-tls.crt --key=/tmp/web-tls.key --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata: {name: nginx}
spec: {controllerName: example.net/gateway-controller}
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: web, namespace: web-app}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: web}}
    spec:
      containers: [{name: nginx, image: nginx:1.27-alpine, ports: [{containerPort: 80}]}]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: web, namespace: web-app}
spec: {selector: {app: web}, ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 80}]}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: web, namespace: web-app}
spec:
  tls: [{hosts: [gateway.web.example], secretName: web-tls}]
  rules:
  - host: gateway.web.example
    http:
      paths:
      - {path: /, pathType: Prefix, backend: {service: {name: web, port: {number: 80}}}}
EOF
questions.meaning: Rebuild the HTTPS Ingress as a Gateway (door + certificate). Add an HTTPRoute (path to service). No Gateway controller runs on Killercoda, so status stays Unknown - that is fine.
questions.words:
• GatewayClass = which controller runs the Gateway
  • Gateway = the entry point
  • listener = port + protocol + hostname (+ TLS certificate)
  • HTTPRoute = rules sending matching requests to a Service
  • parentRefs = the Gateway it attaches to

steps.title: Read the Ingress you must copy

flow.t: kubectl -n web-app get ingress web -o yaml | grep -A12 "^spec"

flow.h: Host, TLS secret and backend move to the new objects.
Gateway must use an existing class.

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' > gw.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata: {name: web-gateway, namespace: web-app}
spec:
  gatewayClassName: nginx
  listeners:
  - name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
    port: 443
    hostname: gateway.web.example
    tls:
      mode: Terminate
      certificateRefs:
      - {kind: Secret, name: web-tls}
EOF

flow.h: Gateway = the entry door with TLS. Ingress host -> listener hostname. Ingress tls.secretName -> certificateRefs. Terminate = the Gateway decrypts HTTPS with that Secret.

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' > route.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: {name: web-route, namespace: web-app}
spec:
  parentRefs: [{name: web-gateway}]
  hostnames: [gateway.web.example]
  rules:
  - matches: [{path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /}}]
    backendRefs: [{name: web, port: 80}]
EOF

flow.h: Route = which traffic goes to which Service (Ingress paths/backend -> rules/backendRefs). parentRefs needs no namespace because the route is in the same namespace as the Gateway.
Migration done; old object removed.

questions.title: NetworkPolicy: choose the least permissive
questions.question:
ssh cka01012
Pods of Deployment frontend (namespace frontend) must be able to reach Pods of Deployment backend (namespace backend) on port 80. A deny-all policy already exists in namespace backend.
Review the NetworkPolicy files in /root/netpol/ and apply the ONE that allows this traffic with the least permissions. Do not delete or modify the existing policies.
questions.meaning: Pick the rule file that opens only the needed door, nothing more.
questions.words:
• NetworkPolicy = a firewall rule for pods
  • default-deny = blocks all incoming traffic to the namespace's pods
  • ingress from = who may connect, picked by namespace label and/or pod label

flow.t: kubectl -n frontend exec deploy/frontend -- wget -qO- -T2 backend.backend

flow.h: Deny-all is in effect. backend.backend = <service>.<namespace>. If this already works, your playground's network plugin ignores NetworkPolicies. Continue anyway. The choice of file is what is graded.

Key rule: in ONE "- from" item, namespaceSelector and podSelector must BOTH match (AND). As separate items, either one is enough (OR). 1 opens everything to all pods. 3 opens all namespaces on all ports. 2 = only frontend pods from namespace frontend, only TCP 80.
Only frontend pods, only port 80.

flow.t: kubectl -n frontend exec deploy/frontend -- wget -qO- -T2 backend.backend | head -4

flow.h: Traffic now allowed.

questions.mug:
kubectl -n frontend exec deploy/frontend -- wget -qO- -T2 backend.backend
cat /root/netpol/*.yaml
kubectl apply -f /root/netpol/policy-2.yaml
kubectl -n frontend exec deploy/frontend -- wget -qO- -T2 backend.backend | head -4
kubectl -n backend get networkpolicy
questions.docs: kubernetes.io: Network Policies (search: namespaceSelector podSelector)

pic.say: Pick the rule file that opens only the needed door, nothing more. Words you need: NetworkPolicy = a firewall rule for pods; default-deny = blocks all incoming traffic to the namespace's pods; ingress from = who may connect, picked by namespace label and/or pod label.

story.broken: A deny-all guard blocks frontend from reaching backend; several rule sheets are offered.
story.fix: Read /root/netpol/*.yaml and apply the least open one that still allows frontend → backend:80.

coach.pattern: Pick the least-permissive NetworkPolicy file and apply it

clues.q: apply the ONE that allows this traffic with the least permissions
clues.means: Read all files; reject ones allowing all pods/namespaces or all ports

clues.q: Do not delete or modify the existing policies
clues.means: Only k apply the chosen file

traps.dont: Apply a file with `namespaceSelector: {}` or no `ports:`
traps.do: Choose the file naming the frontend namespace, frontend Pods and port 80. `{}` means every namespace.

traps.dont: `- namespaceSelector` and `- podSelector` as two separate items
traps.do: Put both selectors in ONE `- from` item. Two items mean OR (too open). One item means AND.
`k apply -f /root/netpol/policy-2.yaml` only, because the task says apply exactly ONE file

verify.cmd: k -n frontend exec deploy/frontend -- wget -qO- -T2 backend.backend | head -4

k -n frontend exec deploy/frontend -- wget -qO- -T2 backend.backend

questions.question:
ssh cka01013
Create a new PriorityClass named urgent for user workloads. Its value must be exactly one less than the highest existing user-defined PriorityClass value (ignore the system-* classes).
Patch the existing Deployment busybox-logger in namespace priority to use PriorityClass urgent. Ensure the Deployment rolls out successfully.

kubectl create namespace priority --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: {name: low-priority}
value: 1000
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: {name: high-priority}
value: 5000
---

One less than 5000.
Pod template now carries the class.

questions.title: HPA with scale-down behavior
questions.question:
ssh cka01014
Create a HorizontalPodAutoscaler named apache-server in namespace autoscale for the existing Deployment apache-server. It must target 50% CPU utilisation per Pod, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 4 replicas. Set the scale-down stabilization window to 30 seconds.
questions.meaning: Auto-add pods when CPU > 50%, and wait 30 s before removing them.
questions.words:
• HPA (HorizontalPodAutoscaler) = changes a Deployment's replica count based on load
  • metrics-server = the add-on that measures pod CPU for it
  • stabilization window = how long the HPA waits before scaling down

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' > hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: apache-server, namespace: autoscale}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: apache-server}
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 4
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: {name: cpu, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 50}}
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 30
EOF

flow.h: behavior only exists in autoscaling/v2 YAML. behavior sits directly under spec, scaleDown under behavior.
<unknown> = no metrics-server is installed in the playground. So there are no CPU numbers yet. The HPA object itself is still correct.

flow.t: kubectl -n autoscale get hpa apache-server -o jsonpath="{.spec.behavior.scaleDown}"

flow.h: Proves behavior was saved. Kubernetes adds the default policies and selectPolicy itself; only the 30 matters.

questions.mug:
cat <<'EOF' > hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: apache-server, namespace: autoscale}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: apache-server}
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 4
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: {name: cpu, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 50}}
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 30
EOF
kubectl apply -f hpa.yaml
kubectl -n autoscale get hpa apache-server
kubectl -n autoscale get hpa apache-server -o jsonpath="{.spec.behavior.scaleDown}"
kubectl -n autoscale get hpa apache-server -o yaml | grep -A4 behavior
questions.docs: kubernetes.io: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (search: stabilizationWindowSeconds behavior)

pic.say: Auto-add pods when CPU > 50%, and wait 30 s before removing them. Words you need: HPA (HorizontalPodAutoscaler) = changes a Deployment's replica count based on load; metrics-server = the add-on that measures pod CPU for it; stabilization window = how long the HPA waits before scaling down.

story.broken: Nobody adds or removes apache-server copies when the kitchen gets busy.
story.fix: Create HPA apache-server: CPU 50%, min 1, max 4, plus the scale-down stabilization window.

coach.pattern: HPA (autoscaling/v2) with scaleDown stabilization window

clues.q: minimum of 1 and a maximum of 4 replicas

traps.do: Put `behavior:` directly under `spec:`, because it sits beside metrics, not inside it
`behavior: scaleDown: stabilizationWindowSeconds: 30`, because the task asks for the scale-down window

traps.dont: `k apply -f hpa.yaml` with no namespace set
traps.do: Set `namespace: autoscale` in metadata, or use `k -n autoscale apply -f hpa.yaml`. Otherwise it lands in default.

questions.title: Default StorageClass with WaitForFirstConsumer
questions.question:
ssh cka01015
Create a StorageClass named local-fast with provisioner rancher.io/local-path and volume binding mode WaitForFirstConsumer. Make it the default StorageClass; it must be the ONLY default. Do not modify existing PersistentVolumeClaims.
questions.setup:
kubectl get deploy -A | grep -q local-path-provisioner || kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rancher/local-path-provisioner/v0.0.30/deploy/local-path-storage.yaml
kubectl patch sc local-path -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"true"}}}'
questions.meaning: Add a storage type and make it the only automatic choice.
questions.words:
• StorageClass = a type of disk Kubernetes can create on demand
  • default class = the one used by a PVC that names no class
  • WaitForFirstConsumer = create the disk only when a pod that uses it is scheduled

flow.h: "(default)" marks the current default. Note EVERY class marked (default).
Remove the old default before adding the new one, so there are never two defaults. Repeat this command for each other class marked (default) in step 1. Change only the name.

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: local-fast
  annotations: {storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"}
provisioner: rancher.io/local-path
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
EOF

flow.h: The annotation (value "true" in quotes) makes it the default.
Exactly one "(default)".

questions.mug:
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl patch sc local-path -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"false"}}}'
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: local-fast
  annotations: {storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"}
provisioner: rancher.io/local-path
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
EOF
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl get sc
questions.docs: kubernetes.io: Change the default StorageClass; Storage Classes (search: is-default-class)

pic.say: Add a storage type and make it the only automatic choice. Words you need: StorageClass = a type of disk Kubernetes can create on demand; default class = the one used by a PVC that names no class; WaitForFirstConsumer = create the disk only when a pod that uses it is scheduled.

story.broken: No room type (StorageClass) local-fast exists, and another class is the default.
story.fix: Create local-fast (local-path, WaitForFirstConsumer), make it default, remove the default mark elsewhere.

coach.pattern: New default StorageClass; un-default all others

clues.q: it must be the ONLY default
clues.means: First patch every old default SC to is-default-class "false", then create local-fast with "true"

traps.dont: Make local-fast default and leave local-path default too
traps.do: Patch every old default to `is-default-class: "false"`, so `k get sc` shows only local-fast (default)

traps.dont: `k delete sc local-path` and recreate it

questions.title: Reuse a retained PV for MariaDB
questions.question:
ssh cka01016
A MariaDB Deployment in namespace mariadb was deleted by mistake, but its PersistentVolume mariadb-pv was kept.
- Create a PersistentVolumeClaim named mariadb in namespace mariadb: access mode ReadWriteOnce, storage 250Mi, so that it binds to the existing PV.
- Edit /root/mariadb-deploy.yaml so the Deployment uses this PVC, then apply it. Ensure the Pod is Running.
questions.setup:
kubectl create namespace mariadb --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata: {name: mariadb-pv}
spec:
  capacity: {storage: 250Mi}
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: ""
  hostPath: {path: /mnt/data/mariadb, type: DirectoryOrCreate}
EOF
cat <<'EOF' > /root/mariadb-deploy.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: mariadb, namespace: mariadb}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: mariadb}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: mariadb}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: mariadb
        image: mariadb:11
        env: [{name: MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD, value: cka}]
        volumeMounts: [{name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/mysql}]
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: ""
EOF
questions.meaning: Make a storage claim that grabs the old disk. Then plug it into the database deployment.
questions.words:
• PV (PersistentVolume) = the disk
  • PVC (PersistentVolumeClaim) = a request for a disk
  • Bound = request matched to a disk
  • RWO (ReadWriteOnce) = one node can mount it read-write

flow.h: Note size, mode and empty class. If STATUS is Released (common in the exam), the PV still remembers its old claim. Run kubectl patch pv mariadb-pv -p '{"spec":{"claimRef":null}}'. Then it becomes Available.

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: mariadb, namespace: mariadb}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: ""
  volumeName: mariadb-pv
  resources: {requests: {storage: 250Mi}}
EOF

flow.h: Empty class "" stops the default class grabbing it. volumeName: mariadb-pv guarantees it binds to exactly that PV.
Bound to the old PV = old data kept.

steps.title: Point the Deployment to the PVC

flow.h: sed -i 's/OLD/NEW/' file = replace text inside the file. Here claimName: "" becomes claimName: mariadb. grep shows the result before you apply.
Database runs on the kept disk.

EOF

questions.title: Kubelet fails: broken systemd drop-in
questions.question:
ssh cka02001
Node node01 is NotReady after a maintenance change. Find out why the kubelet does not start on node01 and fix it. Do not reinstall any packages.
questions.setup:
ssh node01 "sed -i 's#/usr/bin/kubelet #/usr/local/bin/kubelet #' /usr/lib/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf 2>/dev/null; systemctl daemon-reload; systemctl restart kubelet"
sleep 60
questions.meaning: The kubelet service file points to a program path that does not exist; correct it.
questions.words:
• unit file = systemd's recipe for starting a service
  • drop-in = an extra file in kubelet.service.d/ that overrides parts of the main unit
  • daemon-reload = tell systemd to re-read changed unit files. sudo -i = become root (needed in the exam
  • Killercoda is already root)

flow.h: Start from the symptom. If it still says Ready, wait 30 s and run it again. The grace period is ~50 s.

steps.title: Log in, become root and check kubelet

flow.h: 203/EXEC = binary path not found.

flow.t: Failed at step EXEC ... /usr/local/bin/kubelet: No such file

flow.h: Logs show the wrong path.

steps.title: Find the real binary and the config

flow.t:
/usr/bin/kubelet                         (which)
ExecStart=/usr/bin/kubelet               (main unit)
ExecStart=                               (drop-in clears it)
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/kubelet $KUBELET_KUBECONFIG_ARGS ...   (drop-in)

flow.h: The LAST ExecStart wins - it points to /usr/local/bin/kubelet, which does not exist. The real binary is /usr/bin/kubelet.
Each "# /path" line is a file systemd reads. Note the 10-kubeadm.conf path (it may be under /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/ instead).

flow.t: In vim: use the path from the previous step; on the ExecStart= line change /usr/local/bin/kubelet to /usr/bin/kubelet; Esc :wq. Then: active

flow.h: daemon-reload makes systemd re-read the changed file; restart starts kubelet with the right path. Two exits: leave root, leave node01.
Allow ~30s.

questions.question:
ssh cka02002
A new Pod named stuck in namespace default stays Pending, even though nodes have free resources. Diagnose and repair the cluster component responsible so that the Pod is scheduled.
keys: fix the control plane component, not the pod
questions.setup:
sed -i 's#^    - kube-scheduler$#    - kube-schedulerr#' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
sleep 20
kubectl run stuck --image=nginx:1.27-alpine --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

questions.words:

  • static pod = a pod the kubelet runs from a YAML file in /etc/kubernetes/manifests
  • mirror pod = the read-only copy of it you see in kubectl

steps.title: See the pod has no node

flow.h: No events at all = nobody is scheduling.

flow.t: kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep scheduler

flow.t: kubectl -n kube-system describe pod -l component=kube-scheduler | grep -iE 'reason|message'

Reason: StartError (or RunContainerError)
Message: ... exec: "kube-schedulerr": executable file not found in $PATH

flow.h: Typo in the command. crictl logs shows NOTHING here: the program never started, so it printed no log. The error is in the pod status (describe). Or check journalctl -u kubelet | grep scheduler.

flow.h: Files in /etc/kubernetes/manifests need root (exam: sudo -i; Killercoda is already root). sed -i 's#OLD#NEW#' replaces text in the file. kubelet notices the change and recreates the scheduler pod by itself (~30 s).

flow.t: kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep scheduler

kube-scheduler-controlplane 1/1 Running
stuck  1/1  Running ... <any node name>

grep -n "kube-scheduler$" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
exit
kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep scheduler

kubectl get pod stuck -o wide

questions.title: Pending: nodeSelector matches no node
questions.question:
ssh cka02004
Pods of Deployment analytics in namespace data are Pending. Make them run on node01 WITHOUT changing the Deployment.
questions.setup:
kubectl create namespace data --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: analytics, namespace: data}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: analytics}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: analytics}}
    spec:
      nodeSelector: {disktype: ssd}
      containers: [{name: c, image: busybox:1.36, command: [sleep, "3600"]}]
EOF

  • nodeSelector = the labels a pod demands from its node
  • Pending = the scheduler found no node that fits

flow.t: kubectl -n data describe pod -l app=analytics | grep -A3 Events
0/2 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint ...

This is the label to add.
Now node01 matches. --overwrite = replace the value if the label already exists.
Pending pods get scheduled automatically.

kubectl -n data get pods -o wide

kubectl -n data get pods -o wide

questions.title: Init container blocked by missing ConfigMap
questions.question:
ssh cka02005
Deployment inventory in namespace stock never becomes ready. Investigate and fix it. The application expects a ConfigMap named inventory-config with key ready and value yes. Do not modify the Deployment.
questions.meaning: The pod needs a ConfigMap that was never created; create it.
questions.words:
• ConfigMap = a key/value settings object
  • volume = storage mounted into the pod
  • ConfigMap volume = a volume that turns each key into a file
  • init container = a container that must finish before the main one starts

flow.h: Stuck before the main container starts.

flow.t: kubectl -n stock describe pod -l app=inventory | tail -5

flow.h: The pod cannot even mount its volume. So the init container never runs. The ConfigMap behind the volume is missing.
Key "ready" becomes file /config/ready.

flow.t: kubectl -n stock rollout status deploy inventory --timeout=180s

flow.h: Kubelet retries the mount with growing pauses, then the init container finds /config/ready and passes. If it times out, just run it again.

questions.mug:
kubectl -n stock get pods
kubectl -n stock describe pod -l app=inventory | tail -5
kubectl -n stock create configmap inventory-config --from-literal=ready=yes
kubectl -n stock rollout status deploy inventory --timeout=180s
kubectl -n stock get deploy inventory
questions.docs: kubernetes.io: Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap

pic.say: The pod needs a ConfigMap that was never created; create it. story.fix: kubectl create configmap inventory-config --from-literal=ready=yes — the starter step finishes.

clues.means: Create the missing object; don't edit the init container

traps.do: Create the ConfigMap the init container waits for, because modifying the Deployment is forbidden
`--from-literal=ready=yes`, because keys and values are case-sensitive

command -v etcdctl >/dev/null || (apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq etcd-client)

questions.meaning: Save a backup copy of the cluster database into a file.
questions.words:
• etcd = the cluster's database (every object lives there)
  • snapshot = a one-file copy of it
  • CA/cert/key = the ID card etcdctl shows so etcd lets it in. On Killercoda the setup installs a distro etcdctl. It may be older than the cluster's etcd. That is fine for practice.

A table means the file is valid. A "deprecated, use etcdutl" warning is OK.

ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --write-out=table snapshot status /opt/backup/etcd-snap.db
ls -l /opt/backup/etcd-snap.db
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --write-out=table snapshot status /opt/backup/etcd-snap.db

questions.question:

- puts all resources in namespace shop-prod,
- adds the name prefix prod-,

flow.h: Know what you are changing.

flow.t:

resources:
- ../../base
namespace: shop-prod
namePrefix: prod-
replicas:
- name: shop
  count: 3
EOF

Check output before applying.

flow.h: The namespace must exist before the apply. The --dry-run | apply form also works on a re-run. Plain create would say AlreadyExists, which is harmless. -k = apply a kustomization folder.

questions.title: Helm install + upgrade with values
questions.question:
ssh cka02009
Add the Helm repository podinfo (https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo). Install chart podinfo/podinfo version 6.7.1 as release web in namespace helm-web (create it) with 2 replicas.
Then upgrade the release, keeping the same chart version, so that the UI message is "hello cka" (value ui.message). Write the current revision number of the release to /root/helm-rev.txt.
questions.setup: command -v helm >/dev/null || curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash
questions.meaning: Install an app from a Helm chart, then change one setting with an upgrade.
questions.words:
• chart = an app package
  • release = one installed copy of a chart (here = web)
  • revision = the release's version number (1 = install, +1 on every upgrade)

flow.h: Repo = chart catalogue. A chart is an app package; installing it creates a release.

flow.t: helm install web podinfo/podinfo --version 6.7.1 -n helm-web --create-namespace --set replicaCount=2

flow.h: --create-namespace makes helm-web.

flow.t: helm upgrade web podinfo/podinfo --version 6.7.1 -n helm-web --reuse-values --set ui.message="hello cka"

flow.h: --reuse-values keeps replicaCount=2. The question says "keeping the same chart version". So repeat --version 6.7.1. Without it, helm takes the newest chart.
Take the number on the last line (deployed). > writes the output into the file (overwrites it).

questions.mug:
helm repo add podinfo https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo
helm repo update
helm install web podinfo/podinfo --version 6.7.1 -n helm-web --create-namespace --set replicaCount=2
helm upgrade web podinfo/podinfo --version 6.7.1 -n helm-web --reuse-values --set ui.message="hello cka"
helm -n helm-web history web
echo 2 > /root/helm-rev.txt
cat /root/helm-rev.txt
helm -n helm-web get values web
kubectl -n helm-web get deploy
questions.docs: helm.sh docs: helm upgrade (search: --reuse-values --set)

pic.say: Install an app from a Helm chart, then change one setting with an upgrade. Words you need: chart = an app package; release = one installed copy of a chart (here: web); revision = the release's version number (1 = install, +1 on every upgrade).

story.broken: The podinfo meal kit (Helm chart) isn't installed as release web.
story.fix: helm install web podinfo/podinfo 6.7.1 with 2 replicas, then helm upgrade with the new values.

coach.pattern: helm install with --set, upgrade with --reuse-values, read revision

clues.q: version 6.7.1 as release web in namespace helm-web (create it) with 2 replicas
clues.means: helm install web podinfo/podinfo --version 6.7.1 -n helm-web --create-namespace --set replicaCount=2
--set ui.message="hello cka" plus --reuse-values so replicas stay 2
helm -n helm-web history web → last REVISION (2) → echo 2 > /root/helm-rev.txt

traps.do: Add `--reuse-values`, because otherwise replicaCount=2 is dropped and resets to 1
Run `helm upgrade web podinfo/podinfo --version 6.7.1 ...`. Without --version, Helm moves to the newest chart.
Run `echo 2 > /root/helm-rev.txt`. Use the last REVISION from `helm -n helm-web history web`. Only the number is wanted.

Format: HOST/PATH=SERVICE:PORT. The * at the end means pathType Prefix (without it: Exact).

questions.title: TLS ConfigMap: allow only TLSv1.3
questions.question:
ssh cka02011
Deployment nginx-static in namespace nginx-static serves HTTPS using configuration from ConfigMap nginx-config. It currently allows TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3.
Change the configuration so that ONLY TLSv1.3 is accepted, then make the ConfigMap immutable. Make sure the running Pods use the new configuration.
keys: pods must pick up the change
questions.meaning: Edit nginx settings stored in a ConfigMap to allow only TLS 1.3. Lock the ConfigMap. Restart nginx.
questions.words:
• TLS = the encryption behind https (versions 1.2, 1.3)
  • immutable = locked, can never be edited again
  • subPath = mounts one file from a volume, updated only when the pod restarts

steps.title: Wait for nginx, then test TLS 1.2

flow.t: kubectl -n nginx-static rollout status deploy nginx-static
IP=$(kubectl -n nginx-static get svc nginx-static -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'); echo $IP

flow.h: IP=$(...) stores the inner command's output in variable IP; -o jsonpath='{...}' prints one field. curl options: -s = quiet. -k = accept the self-signed cert. --tls-max 1.2 = offer at most TLS 1.2. Baseline: 1.2 is still accepted.
vim opens the ConfigMap. Change the line to   ssl_protocols TLSv1.3;   (keep the ;), then :wq. Change content BEFORE making it immutable.
Immutable = no more edits allowed.

flow.t: kubectl -n nginx-static rollout restart deploy nginx-static && kubectl -n nginx-static rollout status deploy nginx-static

flow.h: subPath files only change on pod restart.
curl -s prints nothing on failure; || echo refused prints 'refused' only when curl fails. Without --tls-max curl uses 1.3 and still gets ok. New shell? Set IP again (step 1).

questions.mug:
kubectl -n nginx-static rollout status deploy nginx-static
IP=$(kubectl -n nginx-static get svc nginx-static -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'); echo $IP
curl -sk --tls-max 1.2 https://$IP
kubectl -n nginx-static edit cm nginx-config
kubectl -n nginx-static patch cm nginx-config -p '{"immutable":true}'
kubectl -n nginx-static rollout restart deploy nginx-static && kubectl -n nginx-static rollout status deploy nginx-static
curl -sk --tls-max 1.2 https://$IP || echo refused
curl -sk https://$IP
kubectl -n nginx-static get cm nginx-config -o jsonpath="{.immutable}"
kubectl -n nginx-static get cm nginx-config -o yaml | grep ssl_protocols
questions.docs: kubernetes.io: ConfigMaps (search: immutable)

pic.say: Edit nginx settings stored in a ConfigMap to allow only TLS 1.3. Lock the ConfigMap. Restart nginx. Words you need: TLS = the encryption behind https (versions 1.2, 1.3); immutable = locked, can never be edited again; subPath = mounts one file from a volume, updated only when the pod restarts.

story.broken: Recipe card (ConfigMap) nginx-config still allows TLSv1.2 and can still be changed.
story.fix: Set TLSv1.3 only, make the ConfigMap immutable, rollout restart nginx-static.

coach.pattern: Edit ConfigMap, make immutable, rollout restart

clues.means: Set immutable: true AFTER the edit (an immutable CM can't be changed)

clues.q: Make sure the running Pods use the new configuration

traps.dont: `k -n nginx-static patch cm nginx-config -p '{"immutable":true}'` before editing
traps.do: Edit to `ssl_protocols TLSv1.3;` first. Then make it immutable. An immutable ConfigMap cannot be edited.

traps.dont: Edit the ConfigMap and stop there
traps.do: Run `k -n nginx-static rollout restart deploy nginx-static`. Running Pods keep the old config until restarted.
`ssl_protocols TLSv1.3;`, because nginx needs the trailing `;` or it fails to start

verify.cmd: k -n nginx-static get cm nginx-config -o yaml | grep ssl_protocols
k -n nginx-static get cm nginx-config -o jsonpath='{.immutable}'

memorise: IP=$(k -n nginx-static get svc nginx-static -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'); curl -sk --tls-max 1.2 https://$IP
k -n nginx-static edit cm nginx-config   # ssl_protocols TLSv1.3;
k -n nginx-static rollout restart deploy nginx-static; k -n nginx-static rollout status deploy nginx-static

questions.title: Write a NetworkPolicy: namespace AND pod selector
questions.question:
ssh cka02012
In namespace db create a NetworkPolicy named db-allow-api that allows incoming traffic to Pods labelled app=db ONLY from Pods labelled role=api in namespace api, on TCP port 80. All other incoming traffic to app=db Pods must be denied.
questions.meaning: Let only the api pods from the api namespace talk to the database. Allow port 80 only.
questions.words:
• NetworkPolicy = a firewall rule for pods
  • ingress = incoming traffic
  • namespaceSelector / podSelector = pick allowed senders by namespace label / pod label

flow.h: cat <<'EOF' > /root/np.yaml ... EOF starts a "heredoc". It writes every line up to EOF into /root/np.yaml. This is the same as pasting into vim. Same list item (no 2nd dash before podSelector) = AND. Once a policy selects app=db pods, every incoming connection it does not allow is denied.

steps.title: Check the network plugin enforces policies

flow.h: Only such plugins enforce NetworkPolicy. If none is listed, the "blocked" test will not time out. That happens even though your YAML is right.

flow.t: kubectl -n api exec api -- wget -qO- -T2 db.db | head -2

flow.h: db.db = Service db in namespace db (short DNS name service.namespace). role=api in ns api passes.

flow.t: kubectl -n api exec web -- wget -qO- -T2 db.db

flow.h: role=web is denied.

questions.mug:
cat <<'EOF' > /root/np.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: db-allow-api, namespace: db}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: db}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: api}}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {role: api}}
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 80}]
EOF
kubectl apply -f /root/np.yaml
kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep -E 'calico|canal|cilium'
kubectl -n api exec api -- wget -qO- -T2 db.db | head -2
kubectl -n api exec web -- wget -qO- -T2 db.db
kubectl -n db describe networkpolicy db-allow-api
questions.docs: kubernetes.io: Network Policies (search: namespaceSelector and podSelector)

pic.say: Let only the api pods from the api namespace talk to the database. Allow port 80 only. Words you need: NetworkPolicy = a firewall rule for pods; ingress = incoming traffic; namespaceSelector / podSelector = pick allowed senders by namespace label / pod label.

story.broken: Anyone can reach the db dishes; only role=api dishes from room api should.
story.fix: NetworkPolicy db-allow-api: namespaceSelector AND podSelector in one from item, TCP 80.

coach.pattern: NetworkPolicy: namespaceSelector AND podSelector in one from item

clues.q: ONLY from Pods labelled role=api in namespace api
clues.means: ONE from item with namespaceSelector (kubernetes.io/metadata.name: api) AND podSelector role: api

traps.dont: `- namespaceSelector: ...` and `- podSelector: ...` as two items
traps.do: One `- namespaceSelector:` item with `podSelector:` under it (no dash), because one item means AND
Add `namespaceSelector` for api, because podSelector alone only matches Pods in namespace db
`matchLabels: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: api`, because Kubernetes puts this label on every namespace automatically

verify.cmd: k -n api exec api -- wget -qO- -T2 db.db | head -2
k -n api exec web -- wget -qO- -T2 db.db

memorise: docs: 'network policies' → copy example → keep Ingress only
podSelector app: db; from: - namespaceSelector: matchLabels kubernetes.io/metadata.name: api   (no dash) podSelector: matchLabels role: api
cat <<'EOF' > /root/np.yaml (or vim) → k apply -f /root/np.yaml; k -n db describe networkpolicy db-allow-api

questions.title: Native sidecar container (restartPolicy Always)
questions.question:
ssh cka02013
Update Deployment order-app in namespace logging: add a sidecar container named log-shipper using image busybox:1.36 that runs: tail -n+1 -F /var/log/order.log
Use the native sidecar pattern (an init container with restartPolicy: Always). Share the log directory using a volume named logs mounted at /var/log in both containers. Do not change the existing container's command.
questions.setup:
kubectl create namespace logging --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: order-app, namespace: logging}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: order-app}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: order-app}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: [sh, -c, "while true; do echo order $(date) >> /var/log/order.log; sleep 3; done"]
EOF
questions.meaning: Add a helper container that keeps reading the app log file through a shared folder. Native sidecars are stable since v1.33.
questions.words:
• init container = runs before the app starts
  • native sidecar = an init container with restartPolicy = Always, running beside the app
  • emptyDir = an empty shared folder that lives as long as the Pod

flow.t: kubectl -n logging get deploy order-app -o yaml > /root/order-app.yaml

flow.h: Backup before big edits (restore with kubectl replace --force -f /root/order-app.yaml).

steps.title: Add the sidecar with kubectl edit

flow.h:
vim opens the live Deployment. Under spec.template.spec, add initContainers and volumes. Add volumeMounts to the existing app container. Do not touch its command. Spaces matter:
spec:
initContainers:
- name: log-shipper
image: busybox:1.36
restartPolicy: Always
command: [sh, -c, "tail -n+1 -F /var/log/order.log"]
volumeMounts:
- {name: logs, mountPath: /var/log}
containers:
- name: app
...existing lines stay...
volumeMounts:
- {name: logs, mountPath: /var/log}
volumes:
- {name: logs, emptyDir: {}}
Save with :wq. If vim reopens with an error at the top, fix the indentation and save again. restartPolicy Always turns the init container into a sidecar.
Sidecar counts as a running container.
Sidecar sees the app log file. (Mounting at /var/log hides busybox's own empty /var/log - harmless.)

questions.mug:
kubectl -n logging get deploy order-app -o yaml > /root/order-app.yaml
kubectl -n logging edit deploy order-app
kubectl -n logging get pods
kubectl -n logging logs deploy/order-app -c log-shipper --tail=3
kubectl -n logging get deploy order-app -o jsonpath="{.spec.template.spec.initContainers[0].restartPolicy}"

pic.say: Add a helper container that keeps reading the app log file through a shared folder. Native sidecars are stable since v1.33. Words you need: init container = runs before the app starts; native sidecar = an init container with restartPolicy: Always, running beside the app; emptyDir = an empty shared folder that lives as long as the Pod.

story.broken: Order-app writes a diary (log) but no helper reads it out.
story.fix: Add log-shipper as an init container with restartPolicy: Always, sharing the log volume.

coach.pattern: Add native sidecar (initContainer, restartPolicy Always) + shared emptyDir

an init container with restartPolicy: Always
clues.means: restartPolicy: Always on the init container

clues.q: a volume named logs mounted at /var/log in both containers
clues.means: volumes: logs emptyDir + volumeMounts in app AND log-shipper

clues.q: Do not change the existing container's command
clues.means: Only add volumeMounts to the app container

traps.do: Add `volumeMounts: - {name: logs, mountPath: /var/log}` to the app container too. Then both share the files.

questions.title: Split node resources evenly across replicas
questions.question:
ssh cka02014
Deployment wordpress in namespace wp runs 3 replicas on node01 (it has an init container). Its Pods stay Pending.
Scale the Deployment to 0. Then give each Pod an equal share of node01's remaining CPU and memory: take node01's allocatable minus what is already requested by other Pods, keep 10% as headroom, and divide the rest by 3. Use identical requests for the init container and the main container. Scale back to 3 and ensure all Pods are Running.
questions.meaning: Share what is free on node01 fairly between 3 pods so all of them fit.
questions.words:
• requests = the CPU/memory the scheduler reserves for a container
  • Allocatable = what node01 can give to pods
  • 1000m (millicores) = 1 CPU, and 1024Ki = 1Mi

steps.title: See why the Pods are Pending

flow.t: kubectl -n wp describe pod -l app=wordpress | grep -m1 Insufficient
Pending ... / FailedScheduling ... Insufficient cpu, Insufficient memory

flow.h: A Pod needs max(biggest init container, sum of main containers). The init container asks 4 CPU / 8Gi - more than node01 has. So no Pod fits, even though the main container is small.
Its own requests must not count while you calculate.

flow.t: kubectl describe node node01 | grep -A7 Allocatable
kubectl describe node node01 | grep -A6 "Allocated resources"

Allocatable: cpu: 1  memory: 1928288Ki (example)
Allocated: Resource Requests Limits / cpu 250m (25%) ... / memory 150Mi (7%) ...

flow.h: Allocatable = what pods may use. In "Allocated resources" take the Requests column (first number), not Limits. cpu 1 = 1000m (cpu 2 = 2000m). Memory is in Ki: Ki ÷ 1024 = Mi. Your numbers will differ - write them down.

$(( ... )) = shell integer arithmetic (it always rounds down). Put YOUR numbers in. Allocatable memory Ki ÷ 1024 = Mi. (allocatable - requested) × 90 / 100 keeps 10% headroom. Then / 3 = one Pod's share.

flow.t: kubectl -n wp set resources deploy wordpress -c init --requests=cpu=225m,memory=519Mi
kubectl -n wp set resources deploy wordpress -c wordpress --requests=cpu=225m,memory=519Mi

flow.h: -c picks the container (the init container too). Use YOUR results from the step before.
All three fit now.

questions.mug:
kubectl -n wp get pods
kubectl -n wp describe pod -l app=wordpress | grep -m1 Insufficient
kubectl -n wp scale deploy wordpress --replicas=0
kubectl describe node node01 | grep -A7 Allocatable
kubectl describe node node01 | grep -A6 "Allocated resources"
echo $(( 1928288 / 1024 ))
echo cpu=$(( (1000 - 250) * 90 / 100 / 3 ))m
echo memory=$(( (1883 - 150) * 90 / 100 / 3 ))Mi
kubectl -n wp set resources deploy wordpress -c init --requests=cpu=225m,memory=519Mi
kubectl -n wp set resources deploy wordpress -c wordpress --requests=cpu=225m,memory=519Mi
kubectl -n wp scale deploy wordpress --replicas=3
kubectl -n wp get pods -o wide
kubectl -n wp get deploy wordpress
kubectl -n wp get deploy wordpress -o jsonpath="{.spec.template.spec.initContainers[0].resources}"
kubectl -n wp get deploy wordpress -o jsonpath="{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}"
questions.docs: kubernetes.io: Resource Management for Pods and Containers (search: requests init containers)

pic.say: Share what is free on node01 fairly between 3 pods so all of them fit. Words you need: requests = the CPU/memory the scheduler reserves for a container; Allocatable = what node01 can give to pods; 1000m (millicores) = 1 CPU, and 1024Ki = 1Mi.

story.broken: Three wordpress dishes fight for node01's space; some can't start.
story.fix: Scale to 0, split node01's free CPU/memory by 3 for app and init containers, scale back.

coach.pattern: Compute requests from node allocatable; set on init + main

clues.means: k scale … --replicas=0 first, so its own requests don't count

clues.q: keep 10% as headroom, and divide the rest by 3
Use identical requests for the init container and the main container
clues.means: k set resources -c init … and -c wordpress … with same values

traps.dont: Set requests only on the wordpress container
traps.do: Also run `k -n wp set resources deploy wordpress -c init --requests=...`. A bigger init request still blocks scheduling.

traps.dont: Use the Capacity numbers from `k describe node node01`
traps.do: Use Allocatable, because Capacity includes resources reserved for the system

traps.dont: Read the Limits column under Allocated resources
traps.do: Read the Requests column, because the scheduler only counts requests

traps.dont: Use Ki values directly, or write M instead of Mi
traps.do: Run `echo $(( <memKi> / 1024 ))` to get Mi. Always write `Mi`. M means 1000-based units.

memorise: ssh cka02014; k -n wp scale deploy wordpress --replicas=0
k describe node node01 | grep -A7 Allocatable; k describe node node01 | grep -A6 'Allocated resources'   # Requests column
echo $(( <memKi> / 1024 ))   # Mi;  echo $(( (<alloc> - <requested>) * 90 / 100 / 3 ))   # cpu in m, memory in Mi

questions.title: PVC Pending: wrong StorageClass
questions.question:
ssh cka02015
PVC logs-pvc in namespace storage-fix stays Pending and Pod log-writer cannot start. Fix it so the PVC is Bound using StorageClass local-path (same name, size 200Mi, ReadWriteOnce) and the Pod is Running.
questions.setup:
kubectl get deploy -A | grep -q local-path-provisioner || kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rancher/local-path-provisioner/v0.0.30/deploy/local-path-storage.yaml
kubectl create namespace storage-fix --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: logs-pvc, namespace: storage-fix}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: fast-ssd
  resources: {requests: {storage: 200Mi}}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: log-writer, namespace: storage-fix}
spec:
  containers:
  - {name: c, image: busybox:1.36, command: [sh, -c, "while true; do date >> /data/log; sleep 5; done"], volumeMounts: [{name: d, mountPath: /data}]}
  volumes: [{name: d, persistentVolumeClaim: {claimName: logs-pvc}}]
EOF
questions.meaning: The storage request names a storage type that does not exist. Recreate it with the right type.
questions.words:
• PVC = a request for a disk
  • StorageClass = the kind of disk and who creates it (here local-path)
  • WaitForFirstConsumer = the disk is made only when a Pod uses the claim

flow.t: kubectl -n storage-fix describe pvc logs-pvc | tail -3

flow.h: The class does not exist. local-path uses WaitForFirstConsumer. It creates the disk only when a Pod uses the claim. So even a correct PVC shows Pending until its Pod exists.

steps.title: Save the Pod, then delete Pod and PVC

flow.t: kubectl -n storage-fix get pod log-writer -o yaml > /root/log-writer.yaml

flow.h: storageClassName cannot be edited on a PVC, so it must be recreated. The Pod goes first. A PVC used by a Pod is not removed. Save the Pod first so you can bring it back unchanged. A plain delete is enough for a Pending pod.

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' > /root/logs-pvc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: logs-pvc, namespace: storage-fix}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: local-path
  resources: {requests: {storage: 200Mi}}
EOF

flow.h: cat <<'EOF' > /root/logs-pvc.yaml ... EOF starts a "heredoc". It writes every line up to EOF into /root/logs-pvc.yaml. This is the same as pasting into vim. Same name, size and mode; right class.

steps.title: Recreate the Pod from the saved file

flow.h: A saved object still carries resourceVersion. The API refuses to create an object that has one. The error says "resourceVersion should not be set on objects to be created". sed deletes that line (and uid). status and creationTimestamp are simply ignored.

flow.t: logs-pvc Bound ... local-path / log-writer 1/1 Running (can take ~30 s)

flow.h: local-path binds when the pod starts.

questions.mug:
kubectl -n storage-fix describe pvc logs-pvc | tail -3
kubectl -n storage-fix get pod log-writer -o yaml > /root/log-writer.yaml
kubectl -n storage-fix delete pod log-writer
kubectl -n storage-fix delete pvc logs-pvc
cat <<'EOF' > /root/logs-pvc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: logs-pvc, namespace: storage-fix}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: local-path
  resources: {requests: {storage: 200Mi}}
EOF
kubectl apply -f /root/logs-pvc.yaml
sed -i '/^  resourceVersion:/d; /^  uid:/d' /root/log-writer.yaml
kubectl apply -f /root/log-writer.yaml
kubectl -n storage-fix get pvc,pod
kubectl -n storage-fix get pvc logs-pvc
kubectl -n storage-fix get pod log-writer

questions.question:
ssh cka02016

questions.meaning: Make a disk, request it, and mount it into a pod.
questions.words:

  • PVC = a request that binds to a matching PV
  • hostPath = a folder on the node where the Pod runs (here usually node01)

flow.t:

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume

  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]

  hostPath: {path: /srv/app-data}
---

  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]

EOF
persistentvolume/app-pv created, persistentvolumeclaim/app-pvc created, pod/app-writer created

flow.t: kubectl get pv app-pv; kubectl -n app-store get pvc,pod

questions.title: API server down after etcd change
questions.question:
ssh cka03001
After a migration, kubectl on the controlplane can no longer reach the cluster ("connection refused"). The kube-apiserver is configured incorrectly. Find the problem and repair the cluster. Do not restore any backup.
keys: etcd client port is 2379 (peer port is 2380)
questions.setup:
sed -i "s#--etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379#--etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2380#" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
sleep 30
questions.meaning: The API server dials the wrong etcd port; change 2380 back to 2379.
questions.words:
• static pod = a pod kubelet runs from a /etc/kubernetes/manifests file, restarted when edited
  • etcd = the cluster database
  • 2379 = etcd client port (for the API server), 2380 = peer port (etcd-to-etcd)

flow.h: sudo -i = become root. It is needed for node files. On Killercoda you already are root, so it is harmless. The kubectl error IS the symptom: the API server is down, so use crictl instead.

flow.t: kube-apiserver Exited, or Running/Created with the ATTEMPT count rising

flow.h: kubelet keeps restarting it. crictl talks to the container runtime directly, without the API server.

flow.t: crictl logs $(crictl ps -a --name kube-apiserver -q | head -1) 2>&1 | tail -5

flow.h: $(...) runs the inner command (finds the container ID) and pastes its output in place. 2>&1 also shows error output. It talks to the etcd PEER port.
2379 is for clients like the apiserver.
kubelet notices the change and restarts the pod.
Press Ctrl+C to leave watch once the line shows Running. Takes ~1 minute.

kubectl get nodes
crictl ps -a | grep kube-apiserver
crictl logs $(crictl ps -a --name kube-apiserver -q | head -1) 2>&1 | tail -5
grep -E "listen-client-urls|listen-peer-urls" /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
grep etcd-servers /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
sed -i 's#--etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2380#--etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379#' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
watch -n3 crictl ps --name kube-apiserver
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get nodes
kubectl -n kube-system get pods

story.broken: The front desk (API server) calls the order book (etcd) on port 2380 instead of 2379.
story.fix: Edit kube-apiserver.yaml: set --etcd-servers back to port 2379 — the front desk answers.

questions.title: NetworkPolicy blocks DNS egress
questions.question:
ssh cka03004
In namespace secure, Pod client can reach Service backend by IP but not by name. Existing NetworkPolicies must stay unchanged. Create an additional NetworkPolicy named allow-dns in namespace secure that allows all Pods in the namespace to send DNS queries (UDP and TCP 53) to the cluster DNS Pods in kube-system.
questions.meaning: A firewall rule blocks name lookups; add a rule that allows DNS only.
questions.words:
• egress = outgoing traffic
  • default-deny-egress blocks everything going out, DNS too
  • DNS = turns a name like backend into an IP (CoreDNS pods, label k8s-app=kube-dns)

flow.t: kubectl -n secure exec client -- wget -qO- -T2 backend
kubectl -n secure exec client -- wget -qO- -T2 $(kubectl -n secure get pod backend -o jsonpath="{.status.podIP}") | head -2

flow.h: The first wget takes a few seconds before "bad address". $(...) pastes the pod IP printed by the inner command (jsonpath prints one field). Classic sign: DNS (port 53) is blocked.
Target for the new rule.

cat <<'EOF' > /root/dns.yaml ... EOF starts a "heredoc". It writes every line up to EOF into /root/dns.yaml. This is the same as pasting into vim. podSelector: {} = every pod in the namespace. Policies add up; this one opens only DNS.

flow.t: kubectl -n secure exec client -- wget -qO- -T3 backend | head -2

flow.h: Name resolves and connects.

questions.mug:
kubectl -n secure exec client -- wget -qO- -T2 backend
kubectl -n secure exec client -- wget -qO- -T2 $(kubectl -n secure get pod backend -o jsonpath="{.status.podIP}") | head -2
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns --show-labels
cat <<'EOF' > /root/dns.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-dns, namespace: secure}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}
    ports:
    - {protocol: UDP, port: 53}
    - {protocol: TCP, port: 53}
EOF
kubectl apply -f /root/dns.yaml
kubectl -n secure exec client -- wget -qO- -T3 backend | head -2
kubectl -n secure get networkpolicy
questions.docs: kubernetes.io: Network Policies (search: egress port 53)

pic.say: A firewall rule blocks name lookups; add a rule that allows DNS only. Words you need: egress = outgoing traffic; default-deny-egress blocks everything going out, DNS too; DNS = turns a name like backend into an IP (CoreDNS pods, label k8s-app=kube-dns).

traps.do: One `- namespaceSelector:` item with `podSelector: k8s-app: kube-dns` under it, because two items mean OR
List both UDP 53 and TCP 53. DNS falls back to TCP for large answers.
`policyTypes: [Egress]` only, because Ingress with no rules blocks all incoming traffic to every Pod

questions.title: CRDs: filter by group + create a custom resource
questions.question:
ssh cka03008
cert-manager CRDs are installed.
- Write the names of all CRDs belonging to API group cert-manager.io, one per line and sorted, to /root/cm-crds.txt.
- Create a ClusterIssuer named selfsigned with apiVersion cert-manager.io/v1 that uses the selfSigned issuer type.
- Save the output of kubectl explain for clusterissuer.spec.selfSigned to /root/selfsigned.txt.
questions.setup: kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.16.2/cert-manager.crds.yaml
questions.meaning: List custom types from one group, create one custom object, save its field help.
questions.words:
• CRD = adds a new object kind to Kubernetes
  • custom resource = an object of that kind (your ClusterIssuer)
  • API group = the family name of the kinds (cert-manager.io). Only the CRDs are installed (no cert-manager controller), so the issuer gets no READY status

flow.t: kubectl get crd -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,GROUP:.spec.group --no-headers | awk '$2=="cert-manager.io"{print $1}' | sort > /root/cm-crds.txt; cat /root/cm-crds.txt

flow.h: custom-columns prints two columns, NAME and GROUP. awk '$2=="cert-manager.io"{print $1}' keeps rows whose 2nd column is exactly cert-manager.io. It prints the 1st column. sort orders them. > saves. acme.cert-manager.io items are a different group.
NAMESPACED false = cluster-wide.

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' > /root/ci.yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata: {name: selfsigned}
spec:
  selfSigned: {}
EOF

flow.h: cat <<'EOF' > /root/ci.yaml ... EOF starts a "heredoc". It writes every line up to EOF into /root/ci.yaml. This is the same as pasting into vim. No namespace: a ClusterIssuer is cluster-wide.
Docs come from the CRD schema.

kubectl api-resources --api-group=cert-manager.io
cat <<'EOF' > /root/ci.yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata: {name: selfsigned}
spec:
  selfSigned: {}
EOF
kubectl apply -f /root/ci.yaml
kubectl explain clusterissuer.spec.selfSigned > /root/selfsigned.txt
cat /root/cm-crds.txt
kubectl get clusterissuer selfsigned
